svg.aria-label: Azure hub-and-spoke topology: the six functions the hub centralises and the shared budgets each creates, the two mandated subnets, the shared SNAT ceiling, the gateway throughput cap and how to scale past it, and the spoke-to-spoke trilemma
svg.title: Hub-and-spoke is an ownership diagram, not a connectivity diagram: every centralisation turns a per-spoke property into a budget every spoke shares
svg.text: Every line on the star is a centralisation — and every centralisation creates a shared budget
WHAT THE HUB CENTRALISES, AND WHAT BECOMES SHARED FATE
Egress through one firewall
the SNAT port budget, so every spoke’s connection ceiling
One cross-premises gateway
throughput and flow limits, regardless of circuit size
One DNS solution
name resolution — a mismatch BLOCKS legitimate traffic
One set of public IPs
the egress identity every partner must allow-list
One hub per region
a regional blast radius
None of these appear on the star diagram. A hub is a REGIONAL resource. This is what the CAF recommends and what landing zones are built on.
THE HUB, AND TWO SUBNETS YOU MUST NAME CORRECTLY
GatewaySubnet
at least /26 = 64 addresses — sized for FUTURE ExpressRoute circuits, not today
AzureFirewallSubnet
at least /26 — and does NOT support network security groups at all.
An NSG standard that says “every subnet” needs this written in as an exception.
Hub holds: firewall as primary egress · VPN or ExpressRoute gateway · Bastion for RDP/SSH without public IPs · monitoring sink.
Spokes may sit in different subscriptions and even different Entra tenants. They do NOT deploy their own gateway —
they use the hub’s, which requires routing configuration. A hub with no gateway is valid if you need no on-prem link.
THE SHARED SNAT CEILING
The number of public IPs attached to the firewall sets the SNAT port budget — and therefore the concurrent
outbound connection ceiling for EVERY spoke. One chatty spoke exhausts it for all of them.
To scale it
attach a NAT Gateway to AzureFirewallSubnet: up to 16 public IPs and a much larger
SNAT pool. Return traffic still flows through the firewall, preserving flow symmetry.
Allow-lists
partners must cover EVERY attached address. Use a public IP PREFIX — otherwise adding
an IP to raise SNAT silently changes the source address someone else’s rule matches on.
Inbound: DNAT is also SNAT-ed, so a published backend sees the firewall, not the client. Recover the client IP upstream via X-Forwarded-For.
THE GATEWAY CAPS YOU REGARDLESS OF WHAT YOU BOUGHT
A single ExpressRoute gateway caps AGGREGATE throughput, caps ANY SINGLE TCP FLOW, and limits
CONCURRENT FLOWS — no matter how much circuit bandwidth is attached.
So a 400 Gbps circuit does nothing for on-prem to Azure traffic if the gateway caps at a fraction of it.
FastPath
is the standard way to use bandwidth above the gateway ceiling, and relieves flow limits too.
But keep the firewall and load balancers IN THE HUB — in a spoke they negate FastPath.
If blocked
scale HORIZONTALLY: several hubs in one region, each with its own gateway, firewall and
circuits, ONE shared Firewall Policy, spokes steered to a hub by address plan.
SPOKE-TO-SPOKE IS A TRILEMMA — PEERING IS NOT TRANSITIVE
VIA HUB NVA
DIRECT PEERING
Latency
adds a hop
no hop — recommended
Inspection
every flow inspected
bypassed entirely
Firewall processing cost
charged
reduced or eliminated
Microsoft’s advice
the default
special circumstances only
The option recommended to MINIMISE LATENCY is the one restricted to SPECIAL CIRCUMSTANCES — because
nothing inspects it. Limit it to spokes in the SAME environment and workload. Both conditions: high-throughput AND low-risk.
Peering counts per VNet are limited, so at scale the mechanism becomes UDRs to a hub appliance. Private Link exposes one resource with no peering at all.
Enabling the hub gateway for spokes takes THREE peering settings, all off by default: Allow gateway transit on the hub, Use the remote gateway on each spoke,
and Allow forwarded traffic on ALL peerings. Direct peering still bills ingress AND egress, so it is a trade against firewall cost, not a saving.
Virtual Network Manager security admin rules are evaluated BEFORE NSG rules, so two NSGs no longer explain a flow on their own.
